entities.name: The Islamic Fiqh, Kalām & Falsafa Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Islamic Fiqh, Kalām & Falsafa Corpus encompasses three interconnected intellectual traditions that developed within Islamic civilization from the 7th–14th centuries CE. Fiqh (jurisprudence) systematized Shari'a law through the four Sunni madhhabs (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and Ja'fari Shi'i law, generating vast legal literature on worship, transactions, family law, criminal law, and statecraft.

Kalām (speculative theology) — practiced by Mu'tazili, Ash'ari, and Maturidi schools — addressed divine attributes, free will, theodicy, and the nature of the Qur'an. Falsafa (Hellenizing philosophy) — represented by al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina (Avicenna), and Ibn Rushd (Averroes) — transmitted and developed Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy.

Ibn Rushd's commentaries on Aristotle became the primary transmission channel for Aristotelian philosophy to medieval Europe, catalyzing the Scholastic revolution.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Islamic Fiqh, Kalām & Falsafa Corpus shaped the intellectual landscape of medieval Islamic civilization, influencing the development of Shari'a law and philosophical thought. Its transmission and adaptation had significant regional impact on Islamic world's jurisprudence and theology.
